title: Food Systems Transformation
text:
← Back to Research overview
Food systems are complex systems spanning the production, processing, transport, distribution, and consumption of food. They deliver nourishment, jobs, community, culture, and pleasure — but today’s food systems do not equitably provide access to sufficient nutritious and safe food for all people, are responsible for a large share of environmental degradation, and are rife with unfair labor practices and human rights violations. Transforming food systems — reshaping the infrastructure, technology, interactions, and actors within them — to become healthy, sustainable, equitable, resilient, and just is essential to addressing problems from human suffering to planetary crisis. This body of work focuses on historical and ongoing food systems change and on policy-relevant food systems information systems and decision-support.
Ongoing
Completed

title: Economics of Agrifood Systems
text:
← Back to Research overview
Agrifood systems are essential to every economy on earth and employ more than a billion people, with billions more dependent on at least one household member’s food system work for their livelihood. Yet statistics on the number of food system workers, the economic value of agrifood systems, and job quality, labor, and human rights remain very limited beyond primary agricultural production. This body of work fills these data gaps as the field’s paradigm shifts from a narrow focus on the agricultural sector to an expanded view of the whole agrifood system, revealing entry points for policies and programs that improve livelihoods and support sustainable, resilient agrifood systems.
Ongoing

title: Home
text:
Kate Schneider Lecy, PhD MPA
Studying the policy and economics of food and nutrition across the globe — in service of a world where everyone has access to enough healthy food from sustainable, ethical, and equitable food systems.
I am an applied economist and public health nutritionist working on healthy food access, equitable and sustainable food systems, and poverty reduction and prosperity, especially for the world’s food producers.
Assistant Professor · School of Sustainability, College of Global Futures · Arizona State University




I hold a PhD in Food Policy and Applied Nutrition from the Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy at Tufts University. Before joining ASU, I was a Research Scholar at the School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS) at Johns Hopkins University. Earlier in my career I spent five years at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation working on agricultural development, and I hold an MPA from the Evans School of Public Policy & Governance at the University of Washington and a BA in Sociology from McGill University.
My work has been published in top journals of applied economics (Food Policy, American Journal of Agricultural Economics), multidisciplinary food journals (Nature Food, Global Food Security), and public health (The Lancet, Public Health Nutrition), among others, and has been supported by funding from the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center, among others.

title: Equitable Access to Healthy & Sustainable Diets
text:
← Back to Research overview
Food security exists when “all people, at all times, have economic, physical, and social access to adequate safe, nutritious foods that meet their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life.” Nearly 30 years after that definition was adopted, hundreds of millions of people remain food insecure, cannot afford a healthy diet, or face other barriers to accessing and choosing healthy foods. This body of work focuses on understanding the constraints to accessing and choosing safe, nourishing, and satisfying foods that promote health and support well-being, and that contribute to more sustainable production systems and value chains — in the US, Rwanda, Malawi, and beyond.
Ongoing

title: Research
text:
My research is grounded in the theory and methods of applied economics, public health nutrition, and data science, and asks one broad question: how do we get from the food systems we have today to food systems — across scales — that are environmentally sustainable, resilient, healthy, equitable, provide for prosperous livelihoods, and are just?
I work in interdisciplinary collaborations to answer specific questions that contribute to this vision, using detailed empirical analysis of primary and secondary, quantitative and qualitative data across the US, low-income countries (primarily sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia), and globally. That work sits within two related, overarching themes:

Equitable access to and consumption of healthy and sustainable diets — including increasing production and consumption of whole grains, legumes, and other “opportunity crops” through demand modeling, price analysis, choice experiments, and survey data analysis.
Agrifood system transformation toward sustainability — split into two connected bodies of work: monitoring and understanding food systems transformation at global and national scales, and filling data gaps in the economics of agrifood systems that these transformations depend on.

Each theme page below covers ongoing and completed projects and links to the publications that came out of them; the full publications list is tagged back to these same themes.




Equitable Access to Healthy & Sustainable Diets
Understanding the constraints to accessing and choosing safe, nourishing, and satisfying foods that promote health and support well-being — in the US, Rwanda, Malawi, and beyond.
Read more →





Food Systems Transformation
Monitoring and understanding historical and ongoing food systems change, and building policy-relevant food systems information systems and decision-support — including leading the data and analysis for the Food Systems Countdown Initiative.
Read more →





Economics of Agrifood Systems
Filling data gaps in the economics of agrifood systems as the field shifts from a narrow focus on agriculture to an expanded view of the whole agrifood system — employment and value added.
Read more →
